prompt: In proteins and peptides, what links the individual amino acid residues together?

choices.text: Amide bonds, called peptide bonds, between the amino group of one residue and the carboxyl of the next
Ester bonds between the carboxyl group of one residue and a side-chain –OH of the next
choices.why: The backbone links are amides formed from amino and carboxyl groups, not esters.

choices.text: Disulfide bonds between every pair of neighboring residues
choices.why: Disulfide bonds form only between cysteine residues and are a second, additional kind of covalent link.

choices.text: Ionic attractions between –NH3^+ and –CO2^− groups
choices.why: Residues are joined covalently by amide (peptide) bonds, not by ionic attractions.

explanation: Proteins and peptides are amino acid polymers in which the residues are linked by amide bonds, or peptide bonds. The amino group of one residue forms an amide bond with the carboxyl of the next, and so on.

prompt: Alanylserine (Ala-Ser) is a dipeptide of alanine and serine. Which groups form its amide bond?

choices.text: The alanine carboxyl and the serine amino group
The serine carboxyl and the alanine amino group
choices.why: That combination gives the other dipeptide, serylalanine (Ser-Ala).

choices.text: The alanine carboxyl and the serine side-chain –OH
choices.why: A peptide bond is an amide, formed with an amino group, not an ester with the –OH.

choices.text: The two amino groups
choices.why: An amide bond joins a carboxyl group to an amino group.

explanation: Alanylserine forms when an amide bond links the alanine carboxyl to the serine amino group. If the alanine amino group reacts with the serine carboxyl instead, serylalanine (Ser-Ala) results.

prompt: In the tripeptide Val-Tyr-Gly, which residue is the C-terminal amino acid, the one with the free –CO2^− group?

choices.text: Gly
Val
choices.why: By convention the N-terminal amino acid, with the free –NH3^+ group, is written on the left, so Val is N-terminal.

choices.text: Tyr
choices.why: Tyr is in the middle; both its amino and carboxyl groups are in amide bonds.

choices.text: It can't be told, because the written order doesn't show which end is which
choices.why: By convention peptides are written with the N-terminal residue on the left and the C-terminal residue on the right.

explanation: By convention, peptides are written with the N-terminal amino acid (free –NH3^+ group) on the left and the C-terminal amino acid (free –CO2^− group) on the right. In Val-Tyr-Gly, Gly is C-terminal.

prompt: How many isomeric tripeptides can be made that each contain valine, tyrosine, and glycine once?
explanation: Exercise 26.4.1: there are six: Val-Tyr-Gly, Tyr-Gly-Val, Gly-Val-Tyr, Val-Gly-Tyr, Tyr-Val-Gly, and Gly-Tyr-Val. Any of the three can be N-terminal, either of the remaining two can be in the middle, and the last is C-terminal: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

prompt: How many different tetrapeptides can be made that each contain alanine, serine, valine, and glycine once?
explanation: As with the tripeptides of Exercise 26.4.1, each ordering is a different peptide because the N-terminal end is written on the left and the C-terminal end on the right. There are 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 orders.

prompt: How is the tripeptide Val-Tyr-Gly written with one-letter abbreviations?

choices.text: VYG
VTG
choices.why: T is threonine; tyrosine is Y.

choices.text: WYG
choices.why: W is tryptophan; valine is V.

choices.text: GYV
choices.why: This reverses the order; GYV is Gly-Tyr-Val, a different tripeptide with Gly at the N-terminus.

explanation: Using Table 26.1.1, Val = V, Tyr = Y, and Gly = G, so Val-Tyr-Gly is VYG (Exercise 26.4.1).

prompt: How many amide (peptide) bonds link the residues in the tetrapeptide M-P-V-G?
explanation: M-P-V-G is Met-Pro-Val-Gly. Four residues in a chain are joined by three amide bonds: Met–Pro, Pro–Val, and Val–Gly (Exercise 26.4.2).

prompt: Why is the amide bond in a peptide planar, with restricted rotation around the C–N bond?

choices.text: Resonance with the carbonyl gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character
The nitrogen is basic and is protonated in the peptide
choices.why: An amide nitrogen is nonbasic, because its lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl group.

choices.text: The C–N bond is a full double bond with no single-bond character
choices.why: The C–N bond has only a certain amount of double-bond character from resonance.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonds between the N–H and C=O of the same amide hold it flat
choices.why: The N–H points 180° away from the C=O; planarity comes from resonance overlap of the nitrogen p orbital with the carbonyl.

explanation: An amide nitrogen is nonbasic because its unshared pair is delocalized by resonance with the carbonyl group. This overlap gives the C–N bond some double-bond character and restricts rotation, so the amide bond is planar and the N–H is oriented 180° to the C=O.

prompt: How is a disulfide linkage, RS–SR, formed between two cysteine residues, and how is it cleaved?

choices.text: Formed by mild oxidation of the thiols; cleaved by mild reduction
Formed by mild reduction of the thiols; cleaved by mild oxidation
choices.why: This is reversed: thiols are oxidized to a disulfide, and the disulfide is reduced back.

choices.text: Formed by amide bond formation; cleaved by hydrolysis
choices.why: Amide bonds join the backbone; the disulfide is an S–S bond made by oxidation.

choices.text: Formed by hydrogen bonding between –SH groups; cleaved by heating
choices.why: A disulfide is a covalent S–S bond made by mild oxidation, not a hydrogen bond.

explanation: A disulfide is formed by mild oxidation of a thiol, RSH, and is cleaved by mild reduction. A disulfide between cysteines in different chains links the chains together; one between cysteines in the same chain forms a loop.

prompt: Insulin is composed of two chains totaling 51 amino acids, linked by two cysteine disulfide bridges. If the A chain has 21 residues, how many residues does the B chain have?
explanation: 51 − 21 = 30. Insulin's A chain has 21 residues and its B chain has 30, and the two chains are linked by disulfide bridges between cysteine residues.
